CALIFORNIA LIMITED PARTNERSHIP FORMATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Ventures, LP · September 5, 2026

FORMATION
Acme Ventures, LP is a limited partnership formed under California law by the filing of a Certificate of Limited Partnership with the office of the California Secretary of State on September 5, 2026. Its general partner is Casey Alex.

CERTIFICATE OF LIMITED PARTNERSHIP — PARTICULARS ON FILE
The Certificate of Limited Partnership filed for Acme Ventures, LP states the following particulars: the street address of its initial principal office is 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814; the name and street address of its initial agent for service of process are Jordan Lee and 456 Oak Ave., Sacramento, CA 95814; and the name and address of its general partner are Casey Alex and 789 Pine St., Sacramento, CA 95814.

FORMATION BY FILING A CERTIFICATE OF LIMITED PARTNERSHIP
California's Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008 requires a specific act to bring a limited partnership into existence: a certificate of limited partnership must be filed with, and on a form prescribed by, the Secretary of State, and the statute pinpoints the moment of formation as the moment the Secretary of State files that certificate — not some earlier date on which the partners may have reached their own agreement. The statute separately requires that the partners have entered into a partnership agreement, either before or after that certificate is filed. The certificate itself must state five specific items: the limited partnership's name (which must comply with the statute's own naming requirement); the street address of its initial principal office; the name and street address of its initial agent for service of process; the name and address of each general partner; and, if different from the principal office address, the limited partnership's mailing address.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In order for a limited partnership to be formed, a certificate of limited partnership must be filed with and on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State and, either before or after the filing of a certificate of limited partnership, the partners shall have entered into a partnership agreement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15902.01(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, certificate of limited partnership required (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&division=&title=2.&part=&chapter=4.5.&article=2.)
  "A limited partnership is formed when the Secretary of State files the certificate of limited partnership."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15902.01(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, moment of formation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&division=&title=2.&part=&chapter=4.5.&article=2.)
  "The certificate must state: (1) the name of the limited partnership, which shall comply with Section 15901.08; (2) the street address of the initial principal office; (3) the name and street address of the initial agent for service of process in accordance with paragraph (1) of subdivision (d) of Section 15901.16; (4) the name and the address of each general partner; and (5) the mailing address of the limited partnership, if different from the address of the initial principal office."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15902.01(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, required content of the certificate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&division=&title=2.&part=&chapter=4.5.&article=2.)
  Known gap: This describes only the formation mechanic and required certificate content stated in Cal. Corp. Code § 15902.01(a) and (c); it does not address that section's other subdivisions — the effect of an inconsistency between the certificate and the partnership agreement (subd. (d)), optional county recording (subd. (e)), cancellation for a dishonored filing-fee payment (subd. (f)), or the annual-tax notice requirement (subd. (g)) — none of which were independently researched for this clause. It also does not state current Secretary of State filing fees, the specific form to use, or where or how to file, none of which are statutory text; that is Secretary of State administrative practice, not verified here. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for a domestic limited partnership formed under the 2008 Act — not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific limited partnership, and not a claim that a foreign limited partnership's California registration (Article 9, §§ 15909.01 et seq.) works identically; that article was not independently verified for this document. This clause is informational only: it does not itself file, or determine the contents of, any specific limited partnership's certificate.

NAMING REQUIREMENT FOR A LIMITED PARTNERSHIP
California's limited partnership statute imposes a specific naming requirement: the name of a limited partnership formed under the Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008 must contain the phrase "limited partnership," or the abbreviation "L.P." or "LP," at the end of its name. The statute separately authorizes, without requiring, a limited partnership's name to include the name of any partner.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) The name of a limited partnership may contain the name of any partner. (b) The name of a limited partnership shall contain the phrase “limited partnership” or the abbreviation “L.P.” or “LP” at the end of its name."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.08(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, name requirements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&division=&title=2.&part=&chapter=4.5.&article=1.)
  Known gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.08(a) and (b). It does not address the statute's separate distinguishability requirement — that the name not be one the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public, and that it be distinguishable in the Secretary of State's records from other limited partnership and reserved names (subd. (d)) — nor the different designator the statute requires of a foreign limited liability limited partnership registering in California, "limited liability limited partnership" or "LLLP"/"L.L.L.P." (subd. (c)), neither of which is independently detailed here. It does not state the Secretary of State's own methodology for comparing names, which is administrative practice rather than statutory text. This clause is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific proposed name complies with this requirement.

GENERAL PARTNERS AND LIMITED PARTNERS — A STRUCTURAL DISTINCTION
California's limited partnership statute builds a basic structural distinction between a limited partnership's two kinds of partners directly into the statutory text. A general partner is, by statute, an agent of the limited partnership for purposes of its activities, and a general partner's act for apparently carrying on the limited partnership's activities in the ordinary course binds the limited partnership, subject to a stated exception for a counterparty who knew or had notice the general partner lacked authority. A limited partner, by contrast, does not have the right or the power, as a limited partner, to act for or bind the limited partnership.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Each general partner is an agent of the limited partnership for the purposes of its activities. An act of a general partner, including the signing of a record in the partnership’s name, for apparently carrying on in the ordinary course the limited partnership’s activities or activities of the kind carried on by the limited partnership binds the limited partnership, unless the general partner did not have authority to act for the limited partnership in the particular matter and the person with which the general partner was dealing knew, had received a notification, or had notice under subdivision (d) of Section 15901.03 that the general partner lacked authority."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.02(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, general partner as agent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&division=&title=2.&part=&chapter=4.5.&article=4.)
  "A limited partner does not have the right or the power as a limited partner to act for or bind the limited partnership."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.02 (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, limited partner has no power to bind (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&division=&title=2.&part=&chapter=4.5.&article=3.)
  Known gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code §§ 15904.02(a) and 15903.02 — the agency/binding-authority rule for each type of partner. It does not address how a person becomes a general partner or a limited partner in the first place (§§ 15903.01, 15904.01), each type's management rights or fiduciary duties, or the statutory exception under which a limited partner who participates in the control of the business can be held liable as if a general partner (addressed separately in this project's limited-partner liability-shield clause). A partnership agreement can shape a specific limited partnership's internal arrangements within the statute's terms; this clause states the statute's own default agency rule, not a description of any specific limited partnership's governing documents or of which role any specific person holds.

THE LIMITED PARTNER LIABILITY SHIELD
California's limited partnership statute states its liability shield for limited partners directly: a limited partner is not liable for an obligation of the limited partnership solely by reason of being a limited partner. The same sentence sets out the shield's own exceptions — it does not protect a person named as a general partner in the certificate, and it does not protect a limited partner who, beyond exercising the rights and powers of a limited partner, participates in the control of the business (a term the statute separately defines through an extensive list of activities that, on their own, do not count as "control"). The statute also states expressly that nothing in the chapter affects a limited partner's own liability to third parties for the limited partner's own tortious conduct.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A limited partner is not liable for any obligation of a limited partnership unless named as a general partner in the certificate or, in addition to exercising the rights and powers of a limited partner, the limited partner participates in the control of the business."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, limited partner not liable for LP obligations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&division=&title=2.&part=&chapter=4.5.&article=3.)
  "Nothing in this chapter shall be construed to affect the liability of a limited partner to third parties for the limited partner’s participation in tortious conduct."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, tortious conduct not affected by the shield (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&division=&title=2.&part=&chapter=4.5.&article=3.)
  Known gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03(a). It does not itemize the statute's extensive safe-harbor list, in subdivision (b), of activities that do not by themselves amount to "participat[ing] in the control of the business" (for example, consulting with a general partner, voting on partnership matters, or serving on a partnership committee); a limited partner's specific conduct and whether it crosses into "control" is a fact-specific question this clause does not answer. It also does not address the narrower liability a limited partner who does participate in control can face under the same subdivision (limited to persons who transacted business with actual knowledge of that participation and a reasonable belief the partner was a general partner), the separate good-faith-investor provision of § 15903.06, or the parallel rules for a foreign limited partnership or a limited liability limited partnership, none of which were independently researched for this clause. This clause is informational only: it does not state whether any specific person's own conduct falls inside or outside this shield.

A GENERAL PARTNER'S OWN LIABILITY FOR PARTNERSHIP OBLIGATIONS
California's limited partnership statute states the converse rule for general partners directly: unless a statutory exception applies, all general partners of a limited partnership are liable jointly and severally for all of the limited partnership's obligations. The statute's own stated exception to that joint-and-several rule is an agreement otherwise reached by the claimant, or a different rule provided elsewhere by law. Separately, a person who becomes a general partner of an already-existing limited partnership is not personally liable for an obligation the limited partnership incurred before that person became a general partner.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (b), all general partners are liable jointly and severally for all obligations of the limited partnership unless otherwise agreed by the claimant or provided by law."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.04(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, general partners jointly and severally liable (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&division=&title=2.&part=&chapter=4.5.&article=4.)
  "A person that becomes a general partner of an existing limited partnership is not personally liable for an obligation of a limited partnership incurred before the person became a general partner."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.04(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, before-admission carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&division=&title=2.&part=&chapter=4.5.&article=4.)
  Known gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.04(a) and (b). It does not address the further collection mechanics of § 15904.05 — including the statute's rule that a judgment against the limited partnership is not by itself a judgment against a general partner, and the specific circumstances (such as an unsatisfied writ of execution against the partnership, or a court's equitable finding) under which a judgment creditor may reach a general partner's own assets — none of which were independently researched for this clause. Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.04 is a separate, independently enacted statutory provision from the general-partnership partner-liability rule this project's General Partnership Agreement document describes elsewhere (Cal. Corp. Code § 16306, in the Uniform Partnership Act of 1994) — the two statutes state a similar joint-and-several rule for their respective entity types, but this clause verifies only the limited-partnership version. This clause is informational only: it does not state whether any specific general partner has personally agreed to different terms with a specific claimant.

PREPARATION AND SIGNATURE BLOCK
This information sheet regarding Acme Ventures, LP was prepared by Jordan Lee.

Executed on September 5, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________
